camp_ilse_ground.text: "You do not read it. You count it." She does not point; she moves her chin. "Three deer paths off that saddle and one of them has prints going both ways. Bracken standing on the north face means nothing has bedded there this week. The water out of the cut runs brown two days after rain and clear on the third, so if it is brown on the fourth, somebody upstream is digging." She stops herself. "You asked a question that has an answer. I am aware I have given you a great deal of it."

choices.label: Give me more of it.

Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_ground_more.text: So she does, for the better part of an hour, and stops only because the fire wants building. It is the most words you have heard out of her at one sitting, and eleven of them are the names of grasses.

camp_ilse_salt.text: "Four pounds does a fortnight. Two for the meat, one for the hides, and one that the road takes off me somewhere between the stall and the ridge, and I have given up finding out where." She turns a stick in the fire. "It is the only thing I buy. The rest the hill gives me or I do without, and there is a great deal I do without, and I would rather you did not make a story out of that."

camp_ilse_salt_carry.text: "You will not," Ilse says, and then hears herself say it. "— You may. Yes. Thank you. I have been on my own long enough that the first answer arrives before I have looked at the question."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_eleven_years.text: "Corran Vale had it thirty-one years and I have had it eleven, and neither of us was paid for the back half," Ilse says. "You have had that. I do not improve it by telling it twice."

choices.label: No.

camp_ilse_eleven_years.text: "There was a warden before me and his name was Corran Vale and he had the hill thirty-one years." She says it the way a date is cut on a stone. "He walked me the whole boundary twice, and then went down to Rivermark to argue for his stipend, and did not come back up it. They had voted the stipend away in the spring and nobody had thought to write and tell him." She turns the stick over. "It has not been paid since. I have had the hill eleven years and been paid for none of them. I am not complaining. I am telling you what a warden is. A warden is whoever has not stopped."

choices.label: Then that town owes you eleven years.
Nobody asked you to stay up here.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_owed.text: "It owes Corran Vale thirty-one," Ilse says. "Start there. He is under the turf by the ford with nothing cut over him. I have thought about cutting something and have not, because he would have called it a wasted afternoon and he would have been right, and I would like to be wrong about it in front of somebody one day."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_nobody_asked.text: "No," Ilse agrees, pleasantly enough. "Nobody asked. That is the arrangement and I have never once misunderstood it." She takes the bow and is forty feet out on the flank again inside a minute, and the fire is a good deal colder for the rest of the night.

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_first_winter.text: "The ford, the fourth night, eighty yards," Ilse says. "You have it. I have not found a way of telling it that comes out better, and I have tried in the dark a number of times."

choices.label: You do not have to tell it better.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_first_winter.text: "Six days, and I was on the north spur for four of them." She is entirely level about it. "They did not come over as a column. They came over in families, at night, in snow, with the small ones tied on. I lay up in the bracken with a bow and a book and counted them, because that is the job, and by the second night I understood that nothing was chasing them — that whatever they were running from was underneath." She stops long enough that the fire shifts. "On the fourth night one of them went through the ice at the ford, eighty yards from where I was lying. I counted her. I did not go down." She looks at the flames rather than at you. "I have given this town four years of very good argument on their behalf and none of it is kindness. It is that I did not go down that night, and it is the only thing I have ever done that is not in the book."

camp_ilse_should_have.text: "Yes," Ilse says. "I know. I have put it to myself in better words than yours." She sets another stick on the fire, squarely, and does not look at you again that evening.

"Counts, dates, weather, what has come up the shaft and when. If I am killed on this hill somebody will find the shelter inside a season, because the salt stall will notice I have stopped coming, and they will lift the stone, because everybody lifts the stone." She holds the book out across the fire without letting go of it for a moment, and then does. "Read it now, then. While I am sitting here. I would like to watch somebody do it."

camp_ilse_the_road.text: Ilse does not look up. "You have had a warden in your camp for a fortnight and Reed has had none in his," she says, and there is no edge on it at all, which is worse. The small book comes out of her coat and opens flat on her knee. "Four in six weeks. All of them on the stretch between the cut and the second ford. All of them loaded going out and none of them touched coming back empty." She turns the book so the firelight is on it, though she does not expect you to read the hand. "Hungry men take the food wagon and go home. These ones let the food wagon pass. Somebody is reading the manifests before the wheels turn, and I can show you where they wait for the ones worth taking. It is not where the watch has been looking."

choices.label: Show me.

camp_ilse_the_names.text: "Eleven names, dated, with what I said and what they answered," Ilse says. "That is the second book and you have had it out of me once, which is once more than anybody else has managed."

choices.label: Then let's decide what happens to it.

camp_ilse_the_names.text: Ilse does not answer at all for long enough that you assume she is not going to. Then she says, "Counts in the one I carry. The one under the stone is not counts." She turns the stick over in the fire. "It is names. Eleven years of who I told, on what day, in what words, and what they said back to me. The reeve twice. The captain before Reed, four times. Three aldermen. A miller. It is written fair, because I write everything fair, and there is a line ruled under each one so that nothing can be added later." She looks at the flames rather than at you. "I have never shown it to anybody. I take it out about twice a year and read it through and put it back, and I have stopped being able to tell whether it is evidence or whether it is a grudge that I have been keeping tidy."

camp_ilse_evidence.text: "Evidence of what," Ilse says, and it is not rhetorical; she waits. "No law was broken. A town declined to act on a warden's advice, which a town is entitled to do, and eleven men said no in eleven perfectly ordinary sentences, and I wrote every one of them down and ruled a line under it." She sets the stick aside. "That is not a case. It is a list of people who disappointed me, kept for eleven years in a fair hand, and I have known that since about the fourth year."

choices.label: Then let's decide what happens to it.

camp_ilse_grudge.text: "Yes," Ilse says at once, and there is nothing defensive in it whatever. "That is the honest reading and it is why I have never shown it to anybody, because the first person who read it would say what you have just said and I would have to agree with them out loud." She is quiet a moment. "Here is the part I cannot get past. Everything in it is true, and it is dated, and it would have been worth having four years ago. A thing can be a grudge and be the only record there is. Nobody has ever told me what one does with that."

choices.label: Then let's decide what happens to it.

camp_ilse_one_entry.text: "The second spring. Alderman Haddon Ferrers, at the market cross, in the afternoon, with two of his people standing off." She does not need the book. "I said: eleven hundred, and four hundred of them cannot fight, and they are coming down because the deep is shut. He said: warden, if there were eleven hundred of anything on that hill we would know about it. I said: you do know about it, I have just told you. He said — and I have this word for word, because I wrote it in the road before I had got out of the square — he said, then write it down somewhere." Ilse puts another stick on the fire, squarely. "So I did. That is the whole of the book and that is the whole of why there is one."

choices.label: He got exactly what he asked for.

camp_ilse_ferrers.text: "He did," Ilse says. "He has had it for nine years and he does not know he has, and about once a season I catch myself hoping he finds out." She looks at the fire. "That is not what a record is for. I am aware."

choices.label: Then let's decide what happens to it.

the_second_book_choice.text: Ilse goes and gets it. It takes her the better part of an hour, and she comes back with the oiled bag under her coat and puts it on the ground between you unopened, which costs her something to do. "Three things and I will not choose," she says. "I have had eleven years to and I have not, and that is the answer to what I am." She counts them off. "Reed can have it. She will read it, and she will act on it, because she is honest and it is the trouble with her — and six of the men in it are the men who vote her budget, and she will spend the rest of her career paying for the afternoon." Two. "Or it goes in the fire, and eleven years of who was told goes with it, and the only account of what this town was warned is the one in their heads." Three. "Or you carry it. Not me. It stops being under my stone and starts being in your pack, and I will have to ask you for it if I want it, and I do not know what that will do to me and I would like to find out."

the_names_to_reed.text: Reed reads four pages standing up in the doorway of the watch house with her cloak still on, and then sits down on the step and reads the rest, and does not say anything for some while. Then she says that six of the names are on her own muster and that two of them signed her commission, and she asks Ilse whether she understands what she has handed over. Ilse says that she does. Reed says that she does not think so, and takes it anyway.

She stands over it the whole way and turns the last of it with the stick so that nothing survives in the ash that a person could read. Afterward she sits down and opens the carried book and writes up the day: weather, distance, what was on the road. Four lines. Nothing else.

"Ask me nothing about it for a month," Ilse says. "After that you may ask me anything you like, and I will probably tell you, and I would rather that were a thing I chose in a month than a thing I said tonight."

after_the_names_kept.text: "One of them will," Ilse says. "Not because he has changed. Because it will one day be cheaper to do the right thing than to argue with you about it, and I have decided that counts, and I have been eleven years deciding it." She sets off up the ridge. camp_ilse_corran_stone.text:
"There is not." Ilse turns the stick in the fire. "Turf by the ford, a thorn that has got away from itself, and eleven years of me walking past it about twice a month."

She is quiet long enough that you take it for the end of the answer, and it is not.

"I know what I would cut. I have had it settled since the third year. His name, thirty-one years, and the word warden, and nothing else on it, because he would have called anything else an advertisement. The mason at Rivermark wants four gold and a fortnight, and I have had four gold twice." She sets the stick down. "I did not go in. I am not going to pretend I know why, and I should be obliged if you did not offer me a reason."

choices.label: Then we cut it. I will carry the stone up the hill myself.
Four gold. Take it to the mason tomorrow.
He would have called it a wasted afternoon.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_corran_cut.text:
"It is nine miles and it is uphill for four of them," Ilse says. "A stone that size is a hundred and forty pounds and you cannot roll it, because the last two miles are bracken over scree."

"I know."

"You do not know. You will." She puts another stick on the fire, squarely. "Very well. Two days, a sledge, and one of us at each end of it, and we do the second half after dark, because the flies on that face in the afternoon are not to be borne."

A pause.

"I have had that planned since the third year as well."

choices.label: This month. Not in the spring.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_corran_dated.text: "This month," Ilse agrees. She takes out the small book and writes it down, dated, in the fair hand — the same hand as the counts, on the same ruled line. "There. Now it is a thing that is happening, rather than a thing I have settled."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_corran_bought.text:
Ilse looks at the four gold in her palm for some while.

"This is the easy half," she says. "I want it understood that I know that. I have had the four gold twice and the difficulty was never the four gold." She closes her hand on it. "It will do. A stone that got there for the wrong reason still has his name on it, and he was a practical man about that sort of thing."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_corran_excuse.text: "He would," Ilse says. "That is what I have told myself for eleven years. It is a very good line and it has kept a stone off a man for a decade." She turns the stick over. "You did not have to hand it back to me."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_believed.text:
"Nobody has." She says it exactly as she says the weather. "Once, arguably. The captain before Reed sent two men up in the fourth year, and they went as far as the cut and came back and wrote that there was nothing — which there was not, on that day, at that hour, at the cut." She turns a stick in the fire. "That is the whole of it. Eleven years of counts, given to eleven people, and the count has never once been the reason for anything."

A pause.

"I stopped expecting it in the fourth year and I have gone on writing them for seven more, and I would rather you did not ask me to account for that, because I cannot."

choices.label: Read me the count now. Whatever is in it, we walk on it tomorrow.
Nobody acts on anything the first time.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_believed_read.text:
She reads it out. It takes forty minutes and it is not interesting, and that is rather the point of it: dates, weather, counts, and the word nothing between them wherever nothing was there.

At the end she closes it and says nothing for a while.

"You will not enjoy tomorrow," she says. "It is nine miles for a thing that will almost certainly not be there." And then, before that can be answered: "I should like to go anyway."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_believed_shrug.text: "The first time," Ilse repeats. "Yes. And the fourth. And the ninth." She sets the stick aside, squarely. "I am aware people mean that kindly. It is an arithmetic that only works if you are not the one doing the counting."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_alone.text:
Ilse works it out honestly, which takes a moment, because she is not going to hand you a number she has not checked.

"A winter and about half the spring after it. The fifth year. The roads shut in the first week of the snow and did not open, and the salt stall does not come up the hill." She turns the stick. "I had a system. I read the count book aloud in the evenings, the whole of it, from the start, so that the voice went on working. By about the fourth week I had stopped doing it for the voice."

She puts the stick on the fire.

"That is a fact about a winter. I should be obliged if you did not make it into anything."

choices.label: Say nothing, and let her decide whether there is more.
That is a terrible thing to hear.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_alone_more.text:
There is more, and it comes about a minute and a half later, in the same level voice.

"I gave the counts names," Ilse says. "The deer. Not all of them — four." She does not look up. "I have never told anybody that, and I am aware of precisely how it sounds, and I am telling you because you did not ask a second question. That has not happened to me before."

She puts another stick on.

"The one with the split ear was called Corran. I am aware of that as well."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_alone_pity.text: "It is a fact about weather," Ilse says. "Do not make it a terrible thing. Then I have to manage you as well, and I have been managing you for four days already over the business at the ford." There is no edge on it whatever, which is how you know it landed.

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_wrong.text:
"The third year. The Ackley boy." She does not have to look it up and does not pretend to. "There is a sett on the north face that has been empty since before I had the hill, and I told his father it was empty, because it was, and I had walked it in the March." The stick turns. "He went up in the August with a lamp and two dogs and came down with his hand opened to the bone."

"An empty sett in March is not an empty sett in August. Everyone knows that. I knew it then. I said empty because it was true when I looked, and because I was in a hurry to be believed about the other thing." She looks at the fire. "That is the whole of it. I write down what I am wrong about as well. It is the same book."

Everybody is wrong sometimes.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_wrong_told.text: "Nobody does," Ilse agrees. "It is in the book, and the book has been under a hearthstone for eleven years, so in practice nobody makes me tell anybody anything." camp_ilse_wrong_shrug.text: "Everybody is," Ilse says. "His hand is not everybody's hand." She sets the stick down, squarely, and does not take up another. "That is the sentence people use to get out of the room. I have used it myself. I am not going to use it about the Ackley boy."

camp_ilse_years.text:
"No." Ilse considers leaving it there and decides not to. "It is not long for me and it is a great while for them, and that is the whole difficulty, and nobody has ever wanted it put that way round."

She turns the stick.

"The reeve who voted the stipend away is dead. His son is dead. His grandson keeps the toll-house at the second ford; he has been perfectly civil to me twice, and he does not know there was a stipend, or a warden before me, or a boundary walk that took two days."

A pause.

"I have not been forgotten by people who decided to forget me. I have been outlived by a town, four times over, in a job it forgot it had."

choices.label: Then the hill is the only thing that remembers it with you.
You will outlast all of it.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_years_hill.text:
"The hill does not remember anything," Ilse says. "It only fails to change quickly."

And then, a good way further into the evening, without looking up: "That is very nearly the same thing, and I have been leaning on it for eleven years, so you may have the point."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_years_outlast.text: "I shall," Ilse agrees. "That is what everyone says, and they say it as though it were the consolation." She puts a stick on the fire, squarely. "Consider what it is you have just told me I have to look forward to."

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_teach.text:
"The tour is an hour, and it is very good, and everybody enjoys it," Ilse says. "The work is a different thing. The work is that you go out before light, at the same hour, on the same line, in whatever the weather is doing, and you write down what is there — and nine days in ten what is there is nothing, so you write nothing, and you go home."

She looks at you properly, which she does not often do.

"That is the entire discipline. There is no other part of it. People want the part where I tell them brown water means somebody is digging. Brown water only means anything because of eleven years of writing down that the water was clear."

choices.label: Before light. Every day. And I carry the book.
When there is time for it.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_teach_terms.text:
"You will carry the book," Ilse repeats, and the order of that sentence pleases her a good deal more than she is going to say. "Very well. Before light. You will be extremely bad at it for about three weeks and I am not going to make that easier for you, and somewhere around the twenty-second day you will see a thing on the line that I have not seen."

She turns the stick over.

"I should like to be there when you do."

choices.label: Wake me an hour early. We start tomorrow.
Back to the fire.

camp_ilse_teach_started.text: She wakes you an hour before light by standing where you are sleeping and saying your name once, which is how she does everything. The line takes two hours. There is nothing on it. She writes nothing, dated, in the fair hand, and hands you the book to carry back.

choices.label: Back.

camp_ilse_teach_later.text: "There is never time for it," Ilse says. "That is not a complaint about you. It is the reason there has been one warden on this hill for forty-two years, and it will be none when I stop." She turns the stick over and does not look up.

choices.label: Back.

ilse_return_sorry.text:
"You should," Ilse agrees, with no heat at all. "That is not the difficulty. A great many people have said that to me at the top of this hill, and every one of them meant it, and I could not tell you what a single one of them did afterwards."

She puts the book away.

"Two things, and then I shall come down or I shall not. The first is a number."

choices.label: Ask it.
Leave her to it.

ilse_return_ask.text: "Then you will not mind two questions," Ilse says. She does not sit down and does not invite you to. "The first is a number."

choices.label: Ask it.
Leave her to it.

ilse_return_number.text:
"I told you how many are under that hill," Ilse says. "I told you at a fire. I told it at a market cross before that, to a man who is now dead. I have told nine other people in eleven years, and not one of them could give it back to me a week later."

She waits.

"How many?"

choices.label: Eleven hundred. Four hundred of them cannot fight.
A great many.
I do not remember.
Leave it.

"A great many," Ilse repeats. "Yes. That is what the alderman said. That is what the captain said. That is what everybody who has ever agreed with me has said, and agreement is not the same as having the number, and the number is the only thing I have."

She opens the book again.

"Come back up when you can say it."

choices.label: Ask me again.
Back down the hill.

ilse_return_number_honest.text:
"No," Ilse says. "Nor did the reeve."

She is quiet a moment, and then does the thing it costs her to do, and says it again.

"Eleven hundred. Four hundred of them cannot fight. They are coming down because the deep is shut." She closes the book. "That is the third time I have given you that. Say it back to me."

choices.label: Eleven hundred. Four hundred of them cannot fight.
Back down the hill.

ilse_return_number_right.text:
Ilse says nothing at all for a moment.

"Yes," she says. "Thank you."

And then, because she is exact and will not let a kindness past unexamined: "That is not proof of anything. A person can learn a number. Which brings me to the second."

choices.label: Go on.

ilse_return_acted.text:
"The second is not a question," Ilse says. "It is a thing I have already checked, because I check everything."

She opens the book to a page near the back and turns it so the light is on it, though she does not expect you to read the hand.

"You went. Whatever else is between us — and there is a good deal — the count was the reason something happened, for the first time in eleven years, and it is written here with the date on it and a line ruled under it, the same as the eleven refusals."

She closes it.

"That is the entry I have wanted since I was given this hill. You are in it. I am not going to pretend it weighs nothing because I am cross with you."

choices.label: Then come down off the hill.
Stay, if the hill needs you.

ilse_return_acted.text:
"The second is not a question either," Ilse says. "It is a condition, and you will not care for it, and I am not going to soften it because you walked nine miles."

She opens the book to a page near the back. There is nothing on it.

"Eleven years. Eleven refusals. A line ruled under each. There is no entry anywhere in it that says somebody went. You have the number now, which is more than the reeve ever managed — and a number nobody walks on is a thing I already have a book full of."

She puts it away.

"Go and act on it. The shaft, the road, the escort; I do not much mind which, and I shall know which. Then come back up, and I shall come down."

choices.label: Say what would count.
Then I will come back.

ilse_return_terms.text: "Anything that costs you the day," Ilse says. "Go down the shaft and shut it, or sound it. Take Reed the count and make her sign for having had it. Walk the road with the wagons instead of behind them." She almost shrugs and does not quite manage it. "It is not a test. It is the job. I have never once been able to explain the difference to anybody and I have given up trying."

choices.label: Back down the hill.

ilse_return_comes.text:
Ilse walks the last quarter mile of the line first, because it is not finished, and writes down what is on it, which is nothing. Then the book goes inside her coat and she picks up the pack that has been standing ready by the shelter door for a good deal longer than she is going to admit to.

"I am not soft about this," she says, on the way down. "You will be told when you are wrong, and it will be in front of the others. That is the arrangement and it is the only one I have."

At the second stile she stops.

"You gave the number back. Nobody has ever given the number back."

choices.label: Down the hill, then.

ilse_close.text: "I have been alone on this hill for eleven years and I had decided that was the shape of it," Ilse says, to the fire, not to you. "I would like to revise that. I am telling you rather than asking you because I have forgotten how the asking goes."

choices.label: Ask me anyway.
Consider it revised.

ilse_close.text: "I walked the boundary this morning out of habit and I was back before you woke," Ilse says, "and I want to tell you that the whole of the last mile of it I was working out how to say a thing, and that I have got about four words." ilse_close.text: Ilse has come in off the flank and sat down at the fire without being asked, and has plainly decided to do it, and is being extremely matter-of-fact about a thing she has not done in eleven years. "Ground and weather are done," she says. "I have nothing left in either of my subjects."

ilse_close.text: Ilse considers the fire for a while and then reports, "Nothing tonight," in the voice she files weather under.

romance_after.text: "Forty feet," Ilse says, out of an hour of nothing. It is the distance she kept off every trail for eleven years. She is sitting close enough that her shoulder moves your sleeve when she breathes. "For the record. I have noticed."

camp_ilse_fate.text: "Sealed is sealed," Ilse says. "I mixed the mortar myself and I know what I put in it." A pause the length of a log settling. "I walk the warren boundary in my head some nights, all the same. That stone is the one piece of ground I ever closed instead of watched. I have not decided which is the worse habit."

choices.label: Watching suits you better.

camp_ilse_fate.text: "We put a sound into the dark and the dark answered," Ilse says, level as ever, "and now the answer is a thing I know, the way I know the fords and the bad ice." She feeds the fire one stick, exactly. "A warden's whole job is knowing what is on her ground. Nobody promised the knowing would be comfortable."

choices.label: Better known than not.
